# Foundations from pandas Time Series

## Learning objectives

By the end of the lesson, students will be able to:

- represent timestamps, periods, frequency, and series identifiers;
- construct and interpret time plots;
- distinguish trend, seasonality, cycles, and irregular variation;
- use seasonal and seasonal-subseries plots;
- explore relationships with scatterplots and scatterplot matrices;
- create and interpret lag plots and ACF plots;
- distinguish structured series from white noise;
- connect visual evidence to forecasting requirements;
- avoid common visual and temporal reasoning errors.

::: {.notes}
Os objetivos são observáveis: cada estudante deverá produzir um gráfico, apontar evidências e explicitar uma implicação para previsão. Tempo: 2 min.
:::


## What can a time coordinate represent?

- **Timestamp:** a specific instant.
- **Fixed period:** a span such as a month or quarter.
- **Interval:** a start and an end.
- **Elapsed time:** distance from an origin.

> The representation must match what the observation actually measures.

::: {.notes}
Use preço de fechamento como exemplo de timestamp e produção mensal como período. Explique que a escolha altera slicing, agregação e labels.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Fixed-frequency and irregular series

::: {.columns}
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Fixed frequency

- every 15 seconds;
- hourly;
- business daily;
- monthly.
:::
::: {.column width="50%"}
### Irregular

- trades;
- incidents;
- publications;
- event records.
:::
:::

A line can display either, but **lag 1 has a stable duration only under a regular calendar**.

::: {.notes}
Em série irregular, shift(1) significa registro anterior, não necessariamente uma hora anterior.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Python date and time objects

```{python}
from datetime import date, time, datetime, timedelta

stamp = datetime(2026, 1, 15, 14, 30)
delta = timedelta(days=2, hours=3)
print(stamp)
print(stamp + delta)
```

- `date`: calendar date;
- `time`: time of day;
- `datetime`: date and time;
- `timedelta`: elapsed duration.

::: {.notes}
Timedelta representa diferença, não uma data.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Parse strings into temporal data

```{python}
raw_dates = pd.Series([
    "2026-01-15", "15/02/2026", "March 20, 2026", "invalid"
])
parsed = pd.to_datetime(
    raw_dates, format="mixed", dayfirst=True, errors="coerce"
)
pd.DataFrame({"raw": raw_dates, "parsed": parsed})
```

`errors="coerce"` exposes failures as missing timestamps. It does not repair their meaning.

::: {.notes}
Discuta ambiguidade entre dia e mês. Prefira formato explícito quando a fonte for estável.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Format timestamps for communication

```{python}
stamp = pd.Timestamp("2026-01-15 14:30")
print(stamp.strftime("%Y-%m-%d"))
print(stamp.strftime("%d %b %Y, %H:%M"))
```

Formatting changes display, not the underlying temporal value.

::: {.notes}
Diferencie armazenamento e apresentação. Labels dependentes de locale podem variar entre ambientes.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## `DatetimeIndex`: time as an analytical axis

```{python}
idx = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=6, freq="D")
series = pd.Series([72, 74, 73, 77, 78, 76], index=idx, name="value")
print(type(series.index).__name__)
series
```

A timestamp-indexed Series supports temporal slicing, frequency logic, shifting, and resampling.

::: {.notes}
O DatetimeIndex é a estrutura central do pandas para séries indexadas por instantes.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Temporal slicing

```{python}
series.loc["2026-01-02":"2026-01-05"]
```

```{python}
daily = pd.Series(
    np.arange(90),
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=90, freq="D")
)
daily.loc["2026-02"].head()
```

Partial strings can select meaningful calendar ranges.

::: {.notes}
Reforce a necessidade de índice temporal ordenado.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Duplicate timestamps require a rule

```{python}
duplicate_time = pd.Series(
    [70, 72, 74, 76],
    index=pd.to_datetime([
        "2026-01-01", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-02", "2026-01-03"
    ])
)
print("unique index:", duplicate_time.index.is_unique)
duplicate_time.groupby(level=0).agg(["mean", "count"])
```

Aggregation resolves duplicates only when the rule is analytically justified.

::: {.notes}
Em preços, mean pode não ser a regra correta. Last, VWAP ou preservação por fonte podem ser alternativas.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Generate regular date ranges

```{python}
print(pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=5, freq="D"))
print(pd.date_range("2026-01-01 00:00", periods=5, freq="15min"))
print(pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=5, freq="B"))
```

Frequency aliases encode calendar rules, not merely display labels.

::: {.notes}
D difer de B. Frequências de negócio não incorporam automaticamente todo calendário local de mercado.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Regularization can introduce missing values

```{python}
irregular = pd.Series(
    [10, 12, 15],
    index=pd.to_datetime(["2026-01-01", "2026-01-03", "2026-01-06"])
)
irregular.asfreq("D")
```

`asfreq` establishes a target calendar. It does not aggregate or justify filling gaps.

::: {.notes}
Compare asfreq com resample. O primeiro expressa frequência; o segundo cria grupos temporais.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Shift values versus shift timestamps

```{python}
shift_demo = pd.Series(
    [100, 102, 101, 105],
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=4, freq="D")
)
print(shift_demo.shift(1))
print(shift_demo.shift(1, freq="D"))
```

- `shift(1)`: moves values relative to the existing index.
- `shift(1, freq="D")`: moves the timestamps by a calendar offset.

::: {.notes}
Essa distinção é central para retornos, lags e alinhamento.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Time zones: localize, then convert

```{python}
naive = pd.date_range("2026-01-15 09:00", periods=3, freq="h")
dublin = naive.tz_localize("Europe/Dublin")
utc = dublin.tz_convert("UTC")
print(dublin)
print(utc)
```

- `tz_localize`: attaches a zone to naive timestamps.
- `tz_convert`: represents the same instants in another zone.

::: {.notes}
Não confunda vincular um timezone com converter instantes já timezone-aware.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## UTC and local calendar features

UTC supports consistent storage and cross-region alignment. Local time remains important for:

- hour-of-day behavior;
- market sessions;
- business operations;
- daylight-saving transitions;
- calendar seasonality.

> Derive seasonal coordinates in the calendar relevant to the phenomenon.

::: {.notes}
A recomendação é separar alinhamento temporal de interpretação sazonal.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Periods represent spans

```{python}
month = pd.Period("2026-01", freq="M")
quarter = pd.Period("2026Q1", freq="Q-DEC")
print(month)
print(month + 2)
print(quarter)
```

Period arithmetic moves across spans according to the declared frequency.

::: {.notes}
Somar dois a uma Period mensal significa avançar dois meses, não segundos.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Convert between timestamps and periods

```{python}
month_ends = pd.date_range("2026-01-31", periods=4, freq="ME")
periods = month_ends.to_period("M")
print(periods)
print(periods.to_timestamp(how="end"))
```

Converting a period to a timestamp requires a boundary convention.

::: {.notes}
Start ou end afeta labels, joins e comparação temporal.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Resampling changes frequency

```{python}
hourly = pd.Series(
    np.arange(24, dtype=float),
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=24, freq="h")
)
hourly.resample("6h").agg(["mean", "max"])
```

- **Downsampling:** higher to lower frequency, usually with aggregation.
- **Upsampling:** lower to higher frequency, usually creating gaps before a filling rule.

::: {.notes}
Mean e max respondem perguntas diferentes. A função de agregação pertence à definição do gráfico.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Interval boundaries matter

```{python}
boundary = pd.Series(
    [1, 2, 3, 4],
    index=pd.to_datetime([
        "2026-01-01 00:00", "2026-01-01 05:59",
        "2026-01-01 06:00", "2026-01-01 11:59"
    ])
)
boundary.resample("6h", closed="left", label="left").sum()
```

`closed` controls interval membership; `label` controls interval naming.

::: {.notes}
Limites temporais são parte da estatística, não apenas detalhe de sintaxe.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Moving windows summarize local history

```{python}
observed = pd.Series(
    [10, 13, 12, 16, 17, 15, 18],
    index=pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=7, freq="D")
)
windows = pd.DataFrame({
    "observed": observed,
    "rolling_mean_3": observed.rolling(3, min_periods=2).mean(),
    "expanding_mean": observed.expanding(min_periods=2).mean(),
    "ewm_mean": observed.ewm(span=3, adjust=False).mean()
})
windows.head()
```

::: {.notes}
Rolling usa memória fixa; expanding acumula desde o começo; EWM reduz pesos gradualmente.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
:::

## Bridge to time series graphics

The pandas toolkit establishes:

- what time means;
- whether the calendar is regular;
- how observations align;
- how frequency changes;
- which values belong to each interval;
- how local summaries are constructed.

Only then can time plots, seasonal plots, lag plots, and ACF plots be interpreted reliably.

::: {.notes}
Use como transição para o conteúdo principal de gráficos de séries temporais.

[Sources]
- https://wesmckinney.com/book/time-series
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Why plotting comes first


> Which visualizations reveal the temporal structures?

**Time order → pattern → seasonality → relationships → dependence → diagnostic judgment**

A time-series graph can reveal:

- changes in level or direction;
- repeating calendar patterns;
- changing variance;
- unusual observations or gaps;
- relationships with exogenous variables;
- persistence and lag structure;
- possible data-quality or timestamp problems.

::: {.notes}

Explique que um gráfico de série temporal não serve apenas para apresentação. Ele orienta hipóteses sobre tendência, sazonalidade, ciclos, eventos incomuns e dependência serial. Tempo: 2 min.

Enfatize que elementos vistos nos gráficos devem ser considerados na escolha ou avaliação do método de previsão. Um gráfico sugere hipóteses, não prova mecanismos causais. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

# Data and Time Structure

## A synthetic electricity-demand dataset

```{python}
hours = pd.date_range("2026-01-01", periods=24 * 90, freq="h")
t = np.arange(len(hours))
hour = hours.hour.to_numpy()
dow = hours.dayofweek.to_numpy() 
day = np.arange(len(hours)) / 24

temperature = 17 + 7 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (hour - 14) / 24) + 3 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * day / 45)
weekend = dow >= 5
daily_cycle = 9 * np.sin(2 * np.pi * (hour - 7) / 24) + 4 * np.sin(4 * np.pi * (hour - 7) / 24)
weekly_effect = np.where(weekend, -8, 0)
trend = 0.025 * day
noise = rng.normal(0, 2.2, len(hours))
demand = 72 + trend + daily_cycle + weekly_effect + 0.35 * (temperature - 17) ** 2 + noise

ts = pd.DataFrame({
    "timestamp": hours,
    "demand_mw": demand,
    "temperature_c": temperature,
    "is_weekend": weekend
})
ts.loc[450, "demand_mw"] += 28
ts.head(3 )
```

::: {.notes}
Explique os componentes apenas após os alunos observarem os gráficos. Há tendência leve, padrões diário e semanal, relação não linear com temperatura, ruído e uma observação incomum intencional. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Observational unit and temporal key

- **Observation:** one hourly market measurement.
- **Time key:** `timestamp`.
- **Target:** `demand_mw`.
- **Covariate:** `temperature_c`.
- **Calendar variable:** `is_weekend`.
- **Declared frequency:** hourly.

```{python}
print(ts.shape)
print(ts.dtypes)
print("unique timestamps:", ts["timestamp"].is_unique)
print("monotonic time:", ts["timestamp"].is_monotonic_increasing)
```

::: {.notes}
A unidade temporal deve ser explícita. Frequência, duplicação e ordenação influenciam todos os gráficos e lags. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Index and columns

```{python}
ts_indexed = ts.set_index("timestamp")
print(ts_indexed.index)
print(ts_indexed.columns)
ts_indexed.head(3)
```

A time index makes ordering, slicing, resampling, and lag construction explicit.

::: {.notes}
Diferencie índice estrutural de uma coluna comum. O índice não substitui a necessidade de verificar frequência e unicidade. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

## Timestamp versus Period

```{python}
print(pd.Timestamp("2026-01"))
print(pd.Period("2026-01", freq="M"))
```

- `Timestamp`: an instant in time.
- `Period`: a span associated with a frequency.

::: {.notes}
Um mês pode representar o primeiro instante do mês ou o intervalo mensal completo. Essa distinção importa para labels, agregações e interpretação. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Frequency is analytical metadata

```{python}
print("inferred frequency:", pd.infer_freq(ts_indexed.index))
print("expected observations:", len(pd.date_range(
    ts_indexed.index.min(), ts_indexed.index.max(), freq="h"
)))
```

A regular frequency defines what “lag 1,” “season,” and “consecutive” mean.

::: {.notes}
Lag 1 em dados horários significa uma hora apenas se o calendário estiver regular. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Detect gaps and duplicate timestamps

```{python}
broken = pd.concat([ts.iloc[:100], ts.iloc[101:110], ts.iloc[[105]]], ignore_index=True)
print("duplicate timestamps:", broken["timestamp"].duplicated().sum())
expected = pd.date_range(broken["timestamp"].min(), broken["timestamp"].max(), freq="h")
missing_timestamps = expected.difference(pd.DatetimeIndex(broken["timestamp"]))
print("missing timestamps:", missing_timestamps.tolist())
```

::: {.notes}
Uma linha unida através de um intervalo ausente pode sugerir continuidade falsa. Verifique o calendário antes de plotar. Tempo: 3 min.
:::

## Reindex to expose missing periods

```{python}
regular = (
    broken.set_index("timestamp")
    .loc[lambda d: ~d.index.duplicated(keep="first")]
    .reindex(expected)
)
regular.loc[regular["demand_mw"].isna()].head()
```

Reindexing makes missing periods explicit; it does not justify interpolation.

::: {.notes}
Diferencie criar a linha ausente no calendário de preencher o valor de demanda. Tempo: 2 min.
:::

# Time Series Graphics

## Why start with graphs?

Graphs help reveal:

- patterns and changes through time;
- unusual observations;
- seasonal behavior;
- relationships between variables;
- temporal dependence.

Visual features should inform the forecasting method considered later.

::: {.notes}
Este material acompanha a sequência e os exemplos gráficos do Capítulo 2, com redação própria. Os exemplos utilizam os arquivos CSV locais informados pelo usuário.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# DataFrame objects

## A time series in a DataFrame

```{python}
df = pd.DataFrame({
    "Year": list(range(2015, 2020)),
    "Observation": [123, 39, 78, 52, 110],
})
df
```

A DataFrame has two labeled axes: an index for rows and columns for variables.

::: {.notes}
Introduza DataFrame, index, columns e dtypes antes dos gráficos.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Index, columns, and data types

```{python}
print(df.index)
print(df.columns)
print(df.dtypes)
print(type(df["Year"]))
```

```{python}
year_df = df.set_index("Year")
year_df
```

::: {.notes}
Uma coluna individual é uma Series. set_index transforma Year em eixo de identificação.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Timestamps and periods

```{python}
print(repr(pd.Timestamp("2020-01")))
print(repr(pd.Period("2020-01", freq="M")))
```

- `Timestamp`: a specific instant.
- `Period`: a span of time with a frequency.

::: {.notes}
A distinção entre instante e período muda a forma como observações mensais são interpretadas.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Timestamp attributes

```{python}
timestamps = pd.date_range("2020-01-01", periods=3, freq="D")
ts_frame = pd.DataFrame(index=timestamps)
ts_frame["date"] = ts_frame.index.date
ts_frame["year"] = ts_frame.index.year
ts_frame["label"] = ts_frame.index.strftime("%A, %B %-d")
ts_frame
```

::: {.notes}
Em Windows, substitua %-d por %#d se necessário.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Key variables identify separate series

```{python}
olympic_running = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "olympic_running_unparsed.csv")
olympic_running.head(3)
```

```{python}
key_columns = ["Length", "Sex"]
olympic_running.groupby(key_columns).size().rename("observations").head(3)
```

A valid multi-series table needs a unique combination of identifying keys and time.

::: {.notes}
No conjunto olímpico, Length e Sex distinguem as séries. Year é a variável temporal.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Wide and long representations

```{python}
wide_demo = olympic_running.pivot_table(
    index="Year", columns=["Length", "Sex"], values="Time"
)
wide_demo.head(3)
```

Long form is convenient for grouped operations and semantic mappings; wide form is useful for matrices and some comparisons.

::: {.notes}
Conecte formato dos dados às bibliotecas de visualização.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme data

```{python}
pbs = (
    pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "PBS_unparsed.csv", parse_dates=["Month"])
    [["Month", "Concession", "Type", "ATC1", "ATC2", "Scripts", "Cost"]]
)
pbs.head()
```

::: {.notes}
O conjunto contém várias séries mensais identificadas por atributos de produto e concessão.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Filter and aggregate one monthly series

```{python}
total_cost_df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "total_cost_df.csv")

a10 = pbs.loc[pbs["ATC2"] == "A10"]
total_cost_df = (
    a10.groupby("Month", as_index=False)
    .agg(Cost=("Cost", "sum"))
    .assign(Cost=lambda x: x["Cost"] / 1e6)
)
total_cost_df.head()
```

::: {.notes}
A agregação transforma várias categorias em uma série mensal de custo total. A unidade passa a milhões de dólares.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## A quarterly multi-series table

```{python}
prison = (
    pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "prison_population.csv", parse_dates=["Date"])
    .rename(columns={"Date": "Quarter"})
    .sort_values(["State", "Gender", "Legal", "Indigenous", "Quarter"])
)
prison.head()
```

```{python}
keys = ["State", "Gender", "Legal", "Indigenous", "Quarter"]
assert not prison.duplicated(keys).any()
```

::: {.notes}
Cada combinação de State, Gender, Legal e Indigenous identifica uma série; Quarter identifica a observação no tempo.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Seasonal period

| Observation interval | Frequent seasonal period |
|---|---:|
| Quarter | 4 |
| Month | 12 |
| Week | about 52 |
| Day | 7 and about 365.25 |
| Hour | 24, 168, and about 8766 |
| Minute | 60, 1440, and 10080 |

A series may contain more than one seasonal pattern.

::: {.notes}
O período sazonal é o número de observações até a repetição do padrão. Calendários reais podem não ser representados exatamente por inteiros simples.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Time plots

## Ansett Airlines

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
ansett = pd.read_csv(
    DATA_PATH / "ansett.csv",
    parse_dates=["ds"],
)

melsyd_economy = (
    ansett
    .loc[
        lambda x:
            (x["Airports"] == "MEL-SYD")
            & (x["Class"] == "Economy")
    ]
    .rename(
        columns={
            "Airports": "unique_id",
        }
    )
    .assign(
        y=lambda x:
            x["y"] / 1000
    )
)

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(10, 5))

ax.plot(
    melsyd_economy["ds"],
    melsyd_economy["y"],
)

ax.set(
    title="Ansett airlines economy class: Melbourne-Sydney",
    xlabel="Week [1W]",
    ylabel="Passengers ('000)",
)

fig.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```


::: {.notes}
O time plot preserva a cronologia. Discuta períodos sem passageiros, mudanças de nível, quedas sazonais e flutuação de longo prazo observáveis no gráfico.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Time-plot reading protocol

Look for:

1. level and long-run direction;
2. fixed-period repetition;
3. changes in variability;
4. unusual observations and gaps;
5. structural breaks or interventions;
6. whether the visible patterns are stable.

::: {.notes}
Descrição visual vem antes de explicação causal.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Time series patterns

## Trend, seasonal, and cyclic behavior

- **Trend:** long-term increase or decrease; it need not be linear.
- **Seasonal:** repetition with a fixed, known, calendar-related period.
- **Cyclic:** rises and falls without a fixed frequency.

A forecasting method should be able to represent the patterns visible in the data.

::: {.notes}
O principal contraste é fixed known period versus duração variável.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Four contrasting patterns

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
aus_production = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "aus_production.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
gafa_stock = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "gafa_stock.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])

fig, axes = plt.subplots(2, 2, figsize=(11, 7))

# Use chapter-compatible local datasets when present.
if (DATA_PATH / "hsales.csv").exists():
    housing = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "hsales.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
    candidate = housing.select_dtypes("number").columns[0]
    axes[0, 0].plot(housing["ds"], housing[candidate])
    axes[0, 0].set_title("Monthly housing sales")
else:
    axes[0, 0].text(.5, .5, "aus_housing.csv not found", ha="center")
    axes[0, 0].set_title("Monthly housing sales")

if (DATA_PATH / "ustreas.csv").exists():
    treasury = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "ustreas.csv")
    ycol = treasury.select_dtypes("number").columns[-1]
    axes[0, 1].plot(treasury[ycol].head(100))
else:
    axes[0, 1].text(.5, .5, "us_treasury.csv not found", ha="center")
axes[0, 1].set_title("US treasury bill contracts")

axes[1, 0].plot(aus_production["ds"], aus_production["Electricity"])
axes[1, 0].set_title("Australian electricity production")

dgoog = (
    gafa_stock.loc[lambda x: (x["unique_id"] == "GOOG_Close") & (x["ds"] >= "2018")]
    .assign(diff=lambda x: x["y"].diff())
)
axes[1, 1].plot(dgoog["ds"], dgoog["diff"])
axes[1, 1].set_title("Daily change in Google closing price")

fig.suptitle("Four examples of time-series patterns")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O capítulo contrasta sazonalidade e ciclo em housing, tendência no treasury, tendência com sazonalidade em electricity e mudanças aparentemente irregulares no preço do Google. Os dois primeiros painéis dependem dos arquivos locais correspondentes.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Seasonal plots

## Monthly seasonal plot

```{python}
#| echo: false
season_cost = total_cost_df.assign(
    Year=total_cost_df["Month"].dt.year,
    Month_num=total_cost_df["Month"].dt.month,
)
years = np.sort(season_cost["Year"].unique())
palette = dict(zip(years, sns.color_palette("husl", len(years))))
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(
    data=season_cost, x="Month_num", y="Cost", hue="Year",
    palette=palette, legend=False, ax=ax
)
ax.set(
    title="Seasonal Plot: Antidiabetic Drug Sales", xlabel="Month",
    ylabel="$ (millions)", xticks=range(1, 13),
    xticklabels=["Jan", "Feb", "Mar", "Apr", "May", "Jun",
                 "Jul", "Aug", "Sep", "Oct", "Nov", "Dec"]
)
for year, group in season_cost.groupby("Year"):
    ax.text(group["Month_num"].iloc[-1] + .1, group["Cost"].iloc[-1], str(year),
            fontsize=8, color=palette[year], va="center")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Ao sobrepor anos, o padrão dentro do calendário fica mais evidente e anos incomuns podem ser identificados.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html

## Multiple seasonal periods

```{python}
vic_elec_df = pd.read_csv(DATA_PATH / "vic_elec.csv", parse_dates=["ds"])
vic_elec_demand = vic_elec_df.loc[vic_elec_df["unique_id"] == "Demand"].copy()
```

Half-hourly demand can show daily, weekly, and annual patterns.

::: {.notes}
A frequência de 30 minutos implica 48 observações por dia e 336 por semana.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Daily seasonal pattern

```{python}
#| echo: false
daily_season = vic_elec_demand.assign(
    hour_minute=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.strftime("%H:%M"),
    day=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.date,
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
sns.lineplot(
    data=daily_season, x="hour_minute", y="y",
    hue="day", palette="husl", legend=False, ax=ax
)
unique_ticks = daily_season["hour_minute"].unique()
step = max(1, len(unique_ticks) // 12)
positions = range(0, len(unique_ticks), step)
ax.set_xticks(list(positions), labels=unique_ticks[::step], rotation=45)
ax.set(title="Electricity Demand: Victoria", xlabel="Time", ylabel="MWh")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Cada linha representa um dia; o eixo horizontal representa a posição dentro do dia.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Weekly seasonal pattern

```{python}
#| echo: false
weekly_season = (
    vic_elec_demand
    .loc[lambda x: x["ds"].between("2012-01-02", "2014-12-28 23:59")]
    .assign(
        day_of_week=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.day_name(),
        week=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.to_period("W").dt.start_time,
    )
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for _, group in weekly_season.groupby("week"):
    group.plot(x="day_of_week", y="y", ax=ax, legend=False, alpha=.25)
ax.set(title="Electricity Demand: Victoria", xlabel="Time", ylabel="MWh")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
O gráfico reorganiza observações pela posição na semana e permite comparar semanas.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Annual seasonal pattern

```{python}
#| echo: false

    day_of_year=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.strftime("%m-%d"),
    year=lambda x: x["ds"].dt.year,
)
fig, ax = plt.subplots()
for year, group in yearly_season.groupby("year"):
    group.plot(x="day_of_year", y="y", ax=ax, label=str(year), alpha=.7)

plt.show()
```

A sazonalidade anual é exibida sobrepondo anos. Muitos pontos e linhas exigem interpretação cuidadosa.

## Correlation measures linear association

$$
r = \frac{\sum_t (x_t-\bar{x})(y_t-\bar{y})}
{\sqrt{\sum_t(x_t-\bar{x})^2}\sqrt{\sum_t(y_t-\bar{y})^2}}
$$

- `r` lies between -1 and 1;
- sign indicates direction;
- magnitude describes linear association;
- nonlinear structure can be strong even when `r` is modest.

::: {.notes}
Use o scatterplot anterior para mostrar por que um coeficiente único pode ser insuficiente.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Different correlations

```{python}
correlations = [-0.9, -0.5, 0, 0.5, 0.9]
fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 5, figsize=(13, 3), sharex=True, sharey=True)
rng = np.random.default_rng(42)
for ax, rho in zip(axes, correlations):
    values = rng.multivariate_normal([0, 0], [[1, rho], [rho, 1]], size=120)
    ax.scatter(values[:, 0], values[:, 1], s=10, alpha=.55)
    ax.set_title(f"r ≈ {np.corrcoef(values.T)[0,1]:.2f}")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Este gráfico recria o conceito da figura com dados simulados e mostra direção e intensidade da associação linear.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Lag plots

## Quarterly beer production

```{python}
#| echo: false
#| fig-align: center
beer = (
    aus_production[["ds", "Beer"]]
    .loc[lambda x: x["ds"] >= "2000"]
    .assign(Season=lambda x: "Q" + x["ds"].dt.quarter.astype("string"))
    .rename(columns={"Beer": "y"})
)
lims = (.95 * beer["y"].min(), 1.05 * beer["y"].max())
colors = dict(zip(beer["Season"].unique(), sns.color_palette("viridis", 4)))
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 3, figsize=(9, 7), sharex=True, sharey=True)
for i, ax in enumerate(axes.flat, start=1):
    lagged = beer.assign(lag=beer["y"].shift(i))
    sns.scatterplot(data=lagged, x="lag", y="y", hue="Season",
                    palette=colors, ax=ax, legend=(i == 6), s=28)
    ax.plot(lims, lims, color=".5", ls="--", lw=1)
    ax.set(title=f"lag {i}", xlabel="", ylabel="", aspect="equal")
    if i != 6 and ax.get_legend() is not None:
        ax.get_legend().remove()
fig.supxlabel("lag(Beer, k)")
fig.supylabel("Beer")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Relações positivas nos lags 4 e 8 refletem sazonalidade trimestral; lags 2 e 6 relacionam picos a vales.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Autocorrelation

## Definition

$$
r_k = \frac{\sum_{t=k+1}^{T}(y_t-\bar{y})(y_{t-k}-\bar{y})}
{\sum_{t=1}^{T}(y_t-\bar{y})^2}
$$

Autocorrelation measures linear association between a series and its lagged values. The collection of coefficients is the ACF.

::: {.notes}
Cada coeficiente resume um dos painéis do lag plot.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Beer autocorrelation coefficients

```{python}
acf_values = sm.tsa.acf(beer["y"], nlags=9, fft=False)
pd.Series(acf_values, name="ACF").to_frame().rename_axis("lag").iloc[1:].head()
```

::: {.notes}
Compare os sinais e magnitudes com a geometria dos lag plots.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Beer ACF

```{python}
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
plot_acf(beer["y"], lags=16, zero=False, bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Autocorrelation Function for Beer", xlabel="lag [1Q]", ylabel="acf")
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
Lag 4 é grande e positivo por sazonalidade; lag 2 tende a ser negativo porque relaciona trimestres opostos.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Trend and seasonality in ACF plots

- trend often produces large positive autocorrelations that decay slowly;
- seasonality produces peaks at seasonal lags;
- trend plus seasonality combines slow decay with repeated seasonal structure.

::: {.notes}
A ACF não substitui o time plot; os dois gráficos respondem perguntas complementares.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

## Antidiabetic sales ACF

```{python}
#| fig-align: center
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(9, 4))
plot_acf(total_cost_df["Cost"], lags=48, zero=False,
         bartlett_confint=False, auto_ylims=True, ax=ax)
ax.set(title="Autocorrelation Function for Antidiabetic Drug Sales",
       xlabel="lag [1M]", ylabel="acf", ylim=(-.3, None))
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```

::: {.notes}
A redução lenta reflete tendência; a forma periódica reflete sazonalidade mensal.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Key takeaways

## Visual diagnostic sequence

1. validate time, identifiers, and frequency;
2. begin with a time plot;
3. identify trend, seasonality, and cycles;
4. reorganize time with seasonal and subseries plots;
5. inspect relationships with scatterplots;
6. inspect serial dependence with lag plots and ACF;
7. compare residual-looking behavior with white noise;
8. convert visual findings into forecasting requirements.

::: {.notes}
O gráfico é parte do raciocínio de forecasting, não apenas uma etapa de comunicação.

[Sources]
- https://otexts.com/fpppy/02-graphics.html
:::

# Exercises

## Core exercises

1. Plot `Bricks`, `Lynx`, `GOOG_Close`, and Victorian `Demand`.
2. Identify the dates of peak closing prices in `gafa_stock`.
3. Plot `Sales`, `AdBudget`, and `GDP` from `tute1.csv`.
4. Explore annual US natural-gas consumption in New England.
5. Create seasonal and subseries plots for quarterly arrivals.
6. Diagnose a selected Australian retail series with time, seasonal, lag, and ACF plots.
